# Purifying selection on the IP₃ receptor is strongest at the gate and filter and weakest in a luminal loop beside them

**Author:** George Dickinson

*Affiliation to be completed before submission.*

Correspondence: george.dickinson@gmail.com

**Running title:** Where purifying selection acts on the IP₃ receptor

**Keywords:** IP₃ receptor; ITPR; purifying selection; codon models;
per-residue conservation; ion channel; missense variants; ClinVar

---

## Abstract

The inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (IP₃R) is the calcium-release
channel of the endoplasmic reticulum, and vertebrates carry three paralogues,
ITPR1, ITPR2 and ITPR3, whose missense variants cause ataxias, anhidrosis and
neuropathy. Where along its 2,700 residues purifying selection acts has not
been measured on alignments deep enough to score a residue. We fitted codon
models to 57 vertebrate coding sequences, each proved to encode the protein
it was aligned as, and computed per-residue conservation on four nested
alignment layers, the deepest holding 249 to 265 genome-derived orthologues of
each human paralogue. All three paralogues are under strong purifying
selection (one-ratio ω 0.0238 to 0.0430), and ITPR1 is the most constrained
and is intensified relative to its sisters (RELAX k = 9.36). Along the
protein, the gate and the selectivity filter are the most conserved elements
in all three paralogues on a composition-free metric, and the gate is
identical between all three human copies. A 50-residue luminal loop inside the pore domain, located from
the structure's membrane geometry rather than from any annotation, is the
least conserved sequence in the receptor; left inside the pore domain it makes
the pore look less constrained than the linkers. Scored as a classifier of
1,753 ClinVar missense records, conservation separates pathogenic from benign
positions best on the family-wide layer (AUC 0.872), and the deep
within-paralogue layer is third of four. Because 1,546 records (88 %) are of
uncertain significance, we release every residue's scores as a
stratification resource and do not use it to call variants.

## Introduction

The inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor is a tetrameric calcium-release
channel of about 2,700 residues per subunit, gated by IP₃ and calcium at a
cytosolic ligand-binding region and conducting through a pore formed by the
last six transmembrane helices of each subunit [1, 2, 3]. Cryo-electron
microscopy has located its working parts at residue resolution: the ten
residues within 4.5 Å of bound IP₃, the selectivity filter, and the
hydrophobic gate at the cytoplasmic end of the pore [4, 3, 5].
Vertebrates carry three paralogues. Missense variants in *ITPR1* cause
spinocerebellar ataxias 15 and 29 and Gillespie syndrome [6, 7, 8, 9], loss of *ITPR2* function abolishes sweating [10], and *ITPR3* variants
cause a demyelinating neuropathy and, in one recurrent case, a multisystem
disorder [11, 12, 13].

Two kinds of evidence say how strongly a protein is held to its sequence, and
they are not the same measurement. A codon model estimates the ratio of
non-synonymous to synonymous substitution rates on a tree [14]. It measures
selection directly, but it needs coding sequences that provably encode the
protein aligned, and it degrades where synonymous sites saturate. Per-residue
conservation measures how dispersed a column of an alignment is [15, 16].
It needs no synonymous signal, but it needs many sequences per column, and a
column of a 2,700-residue protein cannot be scored from the dozen or so
orthologues a representative phylogenetic alignment holds per paralogue.
Population constraint from human variation [17] answers a third question,
about the last few hundred thousand years, and is not what we measure here.

This paper asks where along the IP₃ receptor purifying selection acts. We
answer it on both axes and keep them apart. On the rate axis we fit
one-ratio, branch, branch-site and site models and a relaxation test to the
three vertebrate paralogues, and carry per-site rates onto the human
proteins. On the conservation axis we build orthologue sets deep enough to
score a residue, from one locus per genome per paralogue in a 309-genome
vertebrate sweep, and compare them against a shallow layer that shows what
the representative alignment alone would have given. We then place every
element of the receptor against the same protein's own linkers, test the
measured functional residues against their own elements, and ask whether the
result classifies the family's clinical missense variants.

Three things make the answer less obvious than it looks. The Pfam signature
named after the ligand, PF08709, contains none of the ten measured IP₃
contacts, which sit in MIR and RIH, the domains the family shares with the
ryanodine receptors [18, 19, 20]. The pore domain contains a stretch that
no annotation carries and that behaves unlike the rest of it. And the
clinical record is mostly uncertain, so a classifier trained on it is scored
on very few positions. Each is reported with the control that measures it.

## Results

### All three paralogues are under strong purifying selection

We recovered a coding sequence for all 57 vertebrate IP₃ receptor tips of
the representative alignment, 43 from protein-database cross-references and
14 from genome gene models, and accepted each only if its translation
reproduced the aligned protein; 24 codons that disagreed were masked rather
than kept (Supplementary Fig. 1). The trimmed codon alignment holds 2,459
codons. One-ratio models give ω = 0.02375 for ITPR1, 0.04303 for ITPR2 and
0.04152 for ITPR3 (Fig. 1; Table 1). The least constrained paralogue
therefore accumulates about one non-synonymous substitution for every 23
synonymous ones across a 2,700-residue channel. Removing every genome gene
model moves no estimate by more than 0.0112 (curated-only ω 0.02118, 0.0318
and 0.03714), so the rates are not an artefact of the reconstructed models.

**Synonymous sites are saturated inside a single paralogue.** Across
pairwise comparisons within a paralogue, 161 of 171 ITPR1 pairs, and 373 of
420 pairs over all three, exceed a synonymous distance of 1.5, with median dS
of 5.721, 4.53 and 13.483 for ITPR1, ITPR2 and ITPR3 (Extended Data Fig. 1a).
A single paralogue set spans sharks, teleosts and mammals, so saturation is
reached within the copies and not only between them. Every rate we report is
therefore from a tree-based model, and the pairwise matrix is used only as
this diagnostic.

| | ITPR1 | ITPR2 | ITPR3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| one-ratio ω | 0.02375 | 0.04303 | 0.04152 |
| one-ratio ω, curated sequences only | 0.02118 | 0.0318 | 0.03714 |
| RELAX k (test clade against the other two) | 9.3587 | 0.9085 | 0.8356 |
| branch-site ω₂ on the stem | 5.52937 | 999 (at bound) | 999 (at bound) |
| share of sites in the ω₂ class | 0.1102 | 0.14149 | 0.278 |

*Table 1. Rates of the three paralogues, read from the committed codon-model
tables. Two stems carry an ω₂ at the optimiser's upper bound, which is not an
estimate.*

### ITPR1 is the most constrained paralogue and its selection is intensified

Ranked from most to least constrained, the order is ITPR1, ITPR3, ITPR2.
Two-ratio branch models, each paralogue clade against the rest of the
family, separate every clade from its background after correction across the
whole family of 12 likelihood-ratio tests: ITPR1's foreground ω of 0.0241
against a background of 0.0432 (q = 2.9 × 10⁻⁶³), ITPR2's 0.0435 against
0.0317 and ITPR3's 0.0455 against 0.0308 (Fig. 2a). A relaxation test,
which compares whole ω distributions rather than point estimates [21],
gives the same ordering by a different statistic: selection on ITPR1 is
intensified relative to the other two (k = 9.3587), and relaxed on ITPR2
(k = 0.9085) and ITPR3 (k = 0.8356) relative to theirs (Fig. 2b).
ITPR1 is also the paralogue that carries most of the family's pathogenic
missense record.

**Only the ITPR1 stem carries a branch-site rate the data determine.**
Branch-site model A asks whether a class of sites evolved faster than
neutrally on the stem of a paralogue, the interval in which a new copy was
most free to change [22]. We ran it from four initial ω on every stem, and
3 of the 12 restarts converged below their own nested null, one on every
stem and from a different starting value each time (Extended Data Fig. 1b).
Each of those is a local optimum a single-start run would have reported. All
three stem tests are significant after correction, but only one is
interpretable. On ITPR1 the foreground class has ω₂ = 5.52937 on a share of
0.1102 of sites, stable across the restarts that reach the best likelihood,
with 8 sites above a posterior of 0.95 [23]. On the ITPR2 and ITPR3 stems ω₂
sits at codeml's bound of 999, and on ITPR2 restarts at the same likelihood
place it anywhere from 162 to 999: the stem has no synonymous signal left to
normalise a rate against. Those two tests are significant and their effect
sizes are not measured.

**No site in any paralogue is positively selected.** Within each paralogue,
M2a never gives its positive-selection class a non-zero share, and M8 fits
better than M7 in all three only because it adds a class at exactly ω = 1 on
under 1 % of sites, with 0, 0 and 1 sites reaching a posterior of 0.95. A
class of sites free to drift is not a class being driven.

### The gate and the selectivity filter are the most constrained elements

For per-residue conservation we took one locus per genome per paralogue from
the vertebrate genome sweep, giving 264 ITPR1, 249 ITPR2 and 265 ITPR3
orthologues (Supplementary Fig. 2), and scored each column with a
sequence-weighted Jensen–Shannon divergence [16, 15]. Every element was
tested against the same protein's own linkers, since a whole-protein mean
contains the element being tested. The linker means are 0.7256, 0.7209 and
0.7214.

On the modal-residue fraction, which uses no background model, the gate
and the selectivity filter are the two most conserved elements in all three
paralogues (gate 0.9846, 1.0 and 1.0), with the ITPR1 filter tied with the
RIH-associated domain (Fig. 3; Table 2). On the divergence metric
the gate ranks first in ITPR2 and ITPR3 and second in ITPR1, and the filter
ranks second to fourth. The two are five and seven residues long, so their
tests against the linkers reach p < 0.05 only in ITPR2 and ITPR3 for the gate
(0.0154, 0.0224) and in ITPR3 for the filter (0.0237). The most constrained
whole domain is the RIH-associated domain (0.8037, 0.8016 and 0.7976), and
every named element but one sits above its protein's linker mean.

| element | ITPR1 | ITPR2 | ITPR3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| gate | 0.7994 | 0.822 | 0.822 |
| selectivity filter | 0.7866 | 0.7966 | 0.8114 |
| RIH-associated | 0.8037 | 0.8016 | 0.7976 |
| pore domain, luminal loop removed | 0.7532 | 0.7497 | 0.7489 |
| luminal loop | 0.4883 | 0.4521 | 0.4846 |
| linkers (control) | 0.7256 | 0.7209 | 0.7214 |

*Table 2. Mean Jensen–Shannon divergence per element on the deep layer.
Higher is more conserved.*

### A luminal loop is the least conserved sequence in the receptor

The one exception sits inside the pore domain. We located it from the
structure rather than from any annotation, as the contiguous run of channel
residues whose Cα lies beyond the membrane on the luminal side of the axial
span measured on 6DQN [3]: residues 2401 to 2450 of ITPR3, transferred by
alignment onto ITPR1 and ITPR2, where 49 and 40 of its residues carry a
score. It scores far below every other element and below the
linkers in all three paralogues (0.4883, 0.4521 and 0.4846), and its
modal-residue fraction (0.5468, 0.5632 and 0.5236) says the same without a
background model. On the constraint profile along the pore-forming half, the
curve collapses in the loop and recovers on both sides of it
(Fig. 4).

**Leaving the loop inside the pore domain inverts the pore's result.** With
the loop included, the pore domain read as the least constrained named
element in ITPR1, below the linkers (JSD 0.697, p = 0.96), a strange result
for the pore of an ion channel. We checked three explanations. A metric
artefact was ruled out by the composition-free metric, which gave the same
picture. A gene-model artefact was ruled out by recomputing on the curated
sequences alone, where the loop still scored lowest (0.6191 in ITPR1). The
third explanation held: the domain's mean averaged the most and least
conserved stretches of the receptor. With the loop separated, the pore domain
clears the linker control in all three paralogues (p = 0.0054, 0.0011 and
0.0083). Because the loop was drawn on the membrane's geometry, that result
is not the profile explaining itself.

### The measured functional residues are conserved beyond their own domains

The ten residues within 4.5 Å of IP₃ in 6DQN all fall in MIR and the
N-terminal RIH domain, and none in PF08709, the Pfam signature named after
the ligand. Tested against the whole protein, they are more constrained in
all three paralogues (p = 0.013, 0.0006 and 0.0042). Tested against the rest
of the domains that carry them, the harder control, they are more constrained
in ITPR2 (p = 0.0021) and ITPR3 (p = 0.0253) and higher but not significant
in ITPR1 (p = 0.0697) (Fig. 5a). The filter-lining and gate-lining sets
are two residues each, so we report their means and leave their tests to the
element level, where those elements are powered.

**The gate has not changed in any paralogue since the duplications.**
Identity between the human paralogues, which needs no alignment depth and no
conservation metric, is 1.0 across the five gate residues in all three pairs
(Fig. 5b). The luminal loop retains 0.1304, 0.2041 and 0.3111 identity,
against 0.6405, 0.6628 and 0.7026 for the whole protein. The two extremes of
divergence between the copies therefore lie about fifty residues apart in
the same domain. Measured on the trimmed representative alignment instead,
the whole-protein identities are 0.7526, 0.7728 and 0.812, which is the
difference trimming makes: it keeps 12 of the luminal loop's 51 residues.

**Per-site rates agree on the same coordinates.** Carried onto the human
proteins, FEL [24] calls 5,766 sites purifying across the three paralogues
and one site diversifying, which is inside the procedure's own false
discovery budget. Every gate, filter and contact site in ITPR1 and ITPR3 is
called purifying; in the luminal loop the share falls to 0.2667, 0.3333 and
0.2667 of the codons the trimmed alignment kept, against 0.8603, 0.712 and
0.7733 over the whole protein, with median non-synonymous rates of 0.3275,
0.3902 and 0.3946 where elsewhere they are zero. Painted into the B-factor
column of 16 experimental and predicted structures, both layers show the same
pattern on the channel (Supplementary Fig. 3).

### Conservation separates pathogenic from benign variants, and depth is not the best layer

We placed 1,753 ClinVar missense records on the three canonical sequences
after checking each cited transcript's own translation against the canonical
residue by residue; none was dropped (1,006 ITPR1, 299 ITPR2 and 448 ITPR3
records). A positive control the harvest could have failed passed: both
residue-level variants the literature localises, ITPR3 p.Thr1424Met and
p.Arg2524Cys [11, 13], were recovered. The record is mostly uncertain:
1,546 records are of uncertain significance (875, 261 and 410), and ITPR2's
entire pathogenic record is one position.

The four layers score slightly different sets of residues, so ranking them
on their own coverage would compare the sets as much as the layers. We
therefore scored them on the one fixed set that every layer scores, 44
pathogenic and 34 benign positions (Fig. 6a). The family-wide layer
of 128 IP₃ receptor tips is the best classifier (AUC 0.8723), then the
vertebrate layer (0.8536), then the deep within-paralogue layer (0.758), and
the shallow control is worst (0.6842). Depth was worth building, since the
shallow layer is what the representative alignment alone would have given.
Breadth was worth more: a position conserved across the family's eukaryotic
range and 500 million years of paralogue divergence discriminates better than
one invariant across 260 orthologues of a single gene.

**The ranking holds inside the genes that can be scored.** Without the
restriction to shared positions, the deep layer separates 45 pathogenic from
42 benign positions at AUC 0.7926, higher than on the fixed set, which is why
the restriction matters: each layer's own coverage flatters it differently.
Within ITPR1, which holds most of the labelled positions, the family layer
reaches 0.9013 on the shared set, and within ITPR3 it reaches 0.8533 on five
pathogenic positions. We report no per-gene score for ITPR2, whose single
pathogenic position cannot define a curve.

**The whole-protein control separates two effects.** Each layer also
separates pathogenic positions from the average residue, but by less (0.7574
for the family layer, against 0.8723 for the benign contrast). Part of the
signal is therefore benign calls concentrating in unconstrained positions,
not only pathogenic calls concentrating in constrained ones. Pathogenic
positions are enriched in the gating elements: 2 of ITPR1's pathogenic
positions fall in its five gate residues (odds ratio 48.9, p = 0.0019)
(Supplementary Fig. 4). ITPR1's pathogenic positions cannot be placed
on a structure at all, because neither its rat cryo-electron microscopy
reference nor the AlphaFold DB isoform model carries the human residue at
every shared position.

**Uncertain variants can be stratified, not called.** Against the labelled
distributions of its own gene on the family layer, 58 of 570 scored ITPR1
variants of uncertain significance, 11 of 196 in ITPR2 and 34 of 299 in ITPR3
sit at or above that gene's pathogenic median (Fig. 6b). That says
where a variant sits on an axis the labelled variants separate on. It is not
a pathogenicity call, and the ITPR2 row rests on a single pathogenic
position.

## Discussion

Purifying selection acts on the whole IP₃ receptor, and its strength is not
uniform along it. Two independent axes say where it is strongest. On the rate
axis, a whole-gene ω of 0.02 to 0.04 in every paralogue and a per-site screen
finding thousands of purifying sites and no positively selected one put the
receptor among strongly constrained proteins. On the conservation axis, the
gate and the selectivity filter are the most conserved elements on a
composition-free metric, and the gate is the one element of the channel that
all three paralogues have kept identical since the vertebrate genome
duplications (companion paper 2). The weakest point lies about fifty residues
away, in a luminal loop of the same Pfam domain. The structural literature
places the filter and the gate at the heart of conduction and gating [4, 3, 5], and the conservation pattern agrees with it without having been
told where those elements are: the loop was located from the membrane
geometry, and the filter and gate by transferred structural coordinates with
anchor tests that could have failed.

The loop matters beyond its own score. A per-domain summary is the obvious
way to read a constraint map, and for this channel it gives the wrong answer:
with the loop left in, the pore domain of an ion channel reads as less
constrained than the linkers between its cytosolic domains. Any analysis
that summarises the receptor by Pfam domain will reproduce that artefact,
and the same boundary affects any comparison that uses the pore domain as a
reference. The loop is also where the maps of cryo-electron microscopy are
weakest, which is why we write unscored residues as missing rather than as
unconstrained on the painted structures.

The three copies have not been held to the same standard. ITPR1 is the most
constrained on one-ratio, two-ratio and relaxation tests alike, and its stem
is the only one whose branch-site rate is identifiable, with a class of about
a tenth of sites evolving faster than neutrally on the branch where the copy
was new. ITPR1 also carries almost all of the family's pathogenic missense
record [6, 7, 8, 9]. We do not read the order of the other two as
settled. ITPR2 and ITPR3 differ in one-ratio ω by 0.0015, and ITPR2's near-empty
clinical record is better explained by ascertainment than by tolerance, since
its gate and IP₃ contacts are as conserved as ITPR1's.

For variant interpretation the practical result runs against the design of
the analysis. The deep within-paralogue orthologue sets, which took a
309-genome sweep to build, classify pathogenic against benign positions
better than the shallow control but worse than the family-wide and vertebrate
layers. Conservation across the family's full range, spanning paralogue
divergence and the non-vertebrate grade, is the more informative prior. A
resource for this family should therefore quote the family-wide layer first,
and population constraint [17] would be a separate, complementary axis
rather than a replacement.

**Several limits bound these conclusions.** Synonymous sites are saturated
within every paralogue, so every ω is a tree-based estimate with a soft
denominator, and the two stems whose branch-site rate sits at the
optimiser's bound are unmeasured rather than large. The codon models
condition on the tree and its placement of the paralogue stems
(companion paper 2); a branch test cannot corroborate the topology it is run
on. The rate analyses are vertebrate-only, and nothing here bears on the
single-copy receptors outside the vertebrates (companion paper 1). The deep
layer is about 95 % genome translations; the curated-only recomputation
leaves the element ranking intact but cannot rule out every gene-model
error. The classifier is scored on 44 pathogenic and 34 benign positions,
most of them in ITPR1, so every AUC describes that set rather than the
family's variant space. Conservation and ω measure different things, a
column's dispersion and a substitution-rate ratio, and we report them side by
side without merging them. Finally, the stratification of uncertain variants
is not a classification, and should not be used as one.

## Methods

### Scope

The rate analyses cover the 57 vertebrate IP₃ receptor tips of the
134-sequence representative alignment, which carries the phylogeny of the
family (companion paper 2); the six ryanodine receptor outgroup tips are
excluded because synonymous sites do not survive that distance. The
conservation analyses cover the three human paralogues (UniProt Q14643,
Q14571 and Q14573 [25]) in their own numbering, on four nested layers: a
deep layer of 264, 249 and 265 orthologues of each paralogue, one locus per
genome from a sweep of 309 vertebrate genome assemblies (companion paper 3);
a vertebrate layer of the 57 vertebrate tips; a family-wide layer of all 128
IP₃ receptor tips; and a shallow layer of each paralogue's own
representative tips (19, 13 and 19), kept as the control for what the deep
sets bought. The ryanodine receptors are excluded from every layer, so no
layer scores what the superfamily conserves. The variant analyses cover
every ClinVar missense record on the three genes, 1,753 in all.

### Coding sequences and the codon alignment

Every tip needs a nucleotide sequence that provably encodes its aligned
protein. Candidates came from three routes (Ensembl, UniProt
cross-references and genome gene models from the sweep), and each route was
treated as a generator of candidates rather than an answer, because a UniProt
entry lists every transcript of its gene and for human ITPR1 and ITPR2 the
first listed is not the aligned isoform. Each candidate was translated
against the aligned protein and every disagreement masked to `NNN`, not only
internal stops; 24 codons were masked across the set. Genome gene models were
realigned with miniprot in a mode that keeps frameshift residues [26] and
accepted only if they reproduced the swept protein. PAL2NAL [27] built the
codon alignment, which was cross-checked nucleotide by nucleotide against an
independent in-house protein-to-codon mapping, any disagreement aborting the
build. trimAl [28] columns were chosen on the protein and applied
codon-aware, whole triplets only, keeping 2,459 codons of 3,253. Twelve
constructed negative controls run on every build and check refusal: a
frame-shifted sequence, a sequence encoding a different protein, and a
non-monophyletic foreground must each be refused.

### Selection sets and codon models

The three selection sets are the extended paralogue clades of the maximum
likelihood tree (companion paper 2), re-derived from the rooted tree and
cross-checked against the committed clade table, because a codeml branch
model given a foreground that is not a clade silently marks a larger one.
Six cyclostome tips that the tree places in no paralogue clade stay in the
whole-tree analyses as background and are in no foreground. With PAML 4
[14] we fitted one-ratio models per paralogue and on curated sequences
only, pairwise estimates, a whole-tree one-ratio null, a two-ratio model per
paralogue clade, branch-site model A on each paralogue stem [22], and site
models M1a/M2a and M7/M8 within each paralogue, with Bayes empirical Bayes
posteriors [23]. Branch-site model A was started from ω = 0.5, 1.5, 2.5
and 4 on every stem, and the best restart is reported; the branch-site test
is read against a 50:50 mixture of χ²₀ and χ²₁ because its null sits on a
parameter boundary. Benjamini–Hochberg correction [29] runs across all 12
likelihood-ratio tests together. Pairwise synonymous distances above 1.5 are
flagged as saturated. RELAX [21] in HyPhy [30] tested each paralogue
clade against the other two, leaving unplaced tips unlabelled rather than in
the reference.

### Per-site selection

FEL [24] was run on each paralogue's codon alignment and every site
carried onto the human protein by realignment; a site whose amino acid
disagreed after transfer is written with no residue. Because synonymous
sites are saturated, we report the median non-synonymous rate and the share
of sites called purifying at q < 0.05 per element, and take ω only over sites
whose synonymous rate is identifiable. That rate is unidentifiable at 671 of
7,368 scored sites.

### Orthologue sets and conservation

Deep orthologues were taken from the sweep's gene models at bait coverage
≥ 0.8, identity ≥ 0.4 and at least 1,800 aligned residues, one per genome and
paralogue, with lesion-rich loci excluded. Because bait coverage cannot see
a model that is too long, each sequence was also scored on the fraction of
its own residues landing in reference columns, with the bar placed at the
midpoint of the gap in that distribution (0.7133). It removed one chimeric
model, which had been inflating the ITPR2 alignment from 3,380 to 5,676
columns. Alignments were built with MAFFT L-INS-i [31] at a single thread
for reproducibility. Columns were scored by Jensen–Shannon divergence against
the BLOSUM62 background [15] after position-based sequence weighting
[16], with gaps treated as missing data and the occupancy of each score
reported. A composition-free metric, the modal-residue fraction, and a
recomputation on the curated sequences alone are written beside every
element, not only where a result surprised.

### Elements, controls and functional sites

Pfam elements [32] were taken per accession from InterPro [33] and need
no transfer. The selectivity filter, the gate and the ten IP₃ contacts
(residues within 4.5 Å of IP₃) were measured on the human ITPR3 structure
6DQN [3] and transferred to ITPR1 and ITPR2 by pairwise alignment, each
with an anchor test that aborts rather than writing a coordinate: the filter
must arrive on the GGGVGD motif and the gate on the same lining residues. The
luminal loop was defined geometrically on the same structure. Residues
outside every element were assigned to named linkers and termini, which form
the within-protein control; each element is tested against its protein's
linkers by a one-sided Mann–Whitney test. Functional residues were tested
against the whole protein and against the rest of their own elements.
Identity between paralogues was measured over mutually covered columns of
the untrimmed alignment, with the trimmed-alignment value carried beside it.
Fourteen constructed negative controls run before any table is written,
including a mutated filter motif that the anchor must refuse and a domain
that must not enter the linker control; they were mutation-tested on four
deliberate rule breakages.

### Variants

ClinVar missense records were placed only after each cited transcript's own
translated coding sequence was aligned to the canonical sequence and the
reference amino acid required to match; all three genes file on a transcript
whose translation is the canonical, so none was dropped. The two
residue-level variants localised in the literature must be recovered, as a
positive control. Each layer was scored as a classifier by ROC AUC with a
Mann–Whitney test on three contrasts: pathogenic or likely pathogenic
against benign or likely benign, pathogenic against the whole protein (the
control for ascertainment), and the first contrast restricted to the 44
pathogenic and 34 benign positions every layer scores, which is the contrast
the layers are ranked on. Enrichment by element used Fisher's exact test.
Variants of uncertain significance were stratified against the pathogenic and
benign medians of their own gene, thresholds chosen by the labelled
distributions rather than by us.

### Statistics and reproducibility

Element and site comparisons are one-sided Mann–Whitney tests against the
named control; classifier significance is a Mann–Whitney test on the two
labelled sets. Variant classes were collapsed into pathogenic or likely
pathogenic, benign or likely benign, uncertain, conflicting and other, and
only the first two enter a classifier. No test is reported on fewer than
three observations, which is why the two-residue filter-lining and
gate-lining sets carry means only. A p-value is written with its significant
figures and never rounded to zero. MAFFT runs single-threaded because the
L-INS-i result is not reproducible across thread counts, and every alignment,
table and figure is recorded with its SHA-256 so that a rebuild which drifts
is visible in the data.

### Structures

The deep-layer conservation and the inverted FEL rate were written into the
B-factor column of each IP₃ receptor structure in the panel, with unscored
residues set to −1 so that missing data cannot read as low constraint. A
chain mapping under half of itself to its paralogue was refused. A structure
may carry a human variant position only if every residue it shares with the
human table carries the same amino acid.

## Figure legends

**Fig. 1.** All three paralogues sit more than twenty-fold below
neutrality. Each bar is a paralogue's one-ratio ω from the full codon set,
the bar beside it repeats the estimate with every genome gene model removed,
and the dashed line marks ω = 1. The axis is logarithmic because the result
is the distance below neutrality, which a linear axis would flatten onto the
floor. Removing the reconstructed gene models barely moves any bar, which shows
that they do not drive the rates.

**Fig. 2.** Two statistics on two models separate ITPR1 from its
sisters in the same direction. Panel (a) sets each paralogue clade's
foreground ω against the background ω of the rest of the family in a
two-ratio model. Panel (b) gives the RELAX selection-intensity parameter k
for the same three contrasts, where k above 1 means intensified and below 1
relaxed. A point-estimate contrast and a test on whole rate distributions
agree that ITPR1 is held more tightly than ITPR2 and ITPR3.

**Fig. 3.** The gate and the selectivity filter are the most
conserved elements of the receptor when composition is left out of the
metric, and the luminal loop is the least conserved on both metrics. Panel (a)
ranks every element of the three paralogues by mean Jensen–Shannon
divergence on the deep layer; panel (b) repeats the ranking on the
modal-residue fraction, which uses no background frequencies. Dashed lines
give each protein's linker mean, the within-protein control. The two metrics
agree on the extremes, so neither is a product of scoring transmembrane
residues against a background table.

**Fig. 4.** Conservation collapses in the luminal loop and recovers
on both sides of it in all three paralogues. Each row plots the
modal-residue fraction along the pore-forming half of one paralogue in its
own numbering, in ten-residue bins that never cross an element boundary, so
the edge of the loop is drawn where the structure puts it. The loop, the
filter and the gate are coloured, and the dashed line is that protein's
linker mean. The loop was located from the membrane geometry of 6DQN, so the
dip is a prediction the profile confirms rather than a boundary drawn on it.

**Fig. 5.** The measured functional residues clear the easy control
and most of them clear the hard one. Panel (a) scores the ten IP₃ contacts,
the two filter-lining and the two gate-lining residues against the whole
protein and against the rest of the element each sits in. Panel (b) gives
identity between each pair of human paralogues for every element, with the
gate at full identity in all three pairs and the luminal loop lowest. Beating
the rest of its own element is what shows that the structural annotation
picks out residues its domain does not already share.

**Fig. 6.** The family-wide layer classifies clinical variants
best, and the deep within-paralogue layer ranks third. Panel (a) draws
receiver-operating curves for the four layers on the fixed set of pathogenic
and benign positions that every layer scores, as full curves because the
layers cross. Panel (b) places the variants of uncertain significance on the
same axis against their gene's labelled medians. A resource for this family
should quote the layer at the top of panel (a), and panel (b) is a
stratification, not a call.

## Extended Data

**Extended Data Fig. 1.** Two checks on the codon models show why every rate
here comes from a tree and from the best of several optimiser runs. Panel (a)
plots dN against dS for every pair of tips within each paralogue on log–log
axes, with the neutral diagonal and the saturation bar at dS = 1.5; most
pairs lie past the bar in all three paralogues. Panel (b) plots every
branch-site restart against its own nested null likelihood, and the three
points below the line are local optima that a single-start run would have
reported as answers.

**Supplementary Fig. 1.** The trimmed codon alignment carries every rate in
this paper. Panel (a) plots per-codon occupancy across the 57 tips, marking
the columns trimming kept; panel (b) gives each tip's coverage grouped by the
selection set the tree placed it in; and panel (c) counts the codons that
validation masked, by the route each coding sequence came from. The axis is
in codons, since a nucleotide axis would show a threefold difference that is
not in the data.

**Supplementary Fig. 2.** The deep alignments behind the constraint map
thin out in places, and the figure shows where. Panel (a) counts how many of
the 249 to 265 orthologues cover each residue of the human reference; panel
(b) shows the shape screen, with a ring on the single chimeric model it
removed; panel (c) sets the four conservation layers beside the depth
control. Scores are less reliable where coverage thins than
where it is full.

**Supplementary Fig. 3.** Painting the constraint map onto one
experimental structure of each paralogue shows the most conserved residues
on the pore and leaves the luminal loop grey. Panels (a) to (c) colour each
trace from the B-factor column the painting step wrote, and panel (d) paints
the per-site selection layer onto ITPR3. Unscored residues appear in grey
rather than at the low end of the scale, which keeps missing data from
reading as an absence of constraint in the loop, where the two coincide.

**Supplementary Fig. 4.** Pathogenic positions concentrate in the
elements that gate and select. Panels (a) and (b) place every labelled
variant on the ITPR2 and ITPR3 structures allowed to carry a human position;
panel (c) records the numbering rule for each candidate structure, which the
two ITPR1 structures fail; and panel (d) tests the enrichment of pathogenic
positions per element, with a ring where the test survives correction.
An infinite odds ratio is drawn at the ceiling with a marker so that the
strongest enrichment stays on the axes.

## Data availability

Every table, alignment, tree, figure and report this paper rests on is in
the deposited archive, listed file by file with its size and SHA-256 in
`papers/constraint/deposit_manifest.tsv`. The primary results are
`results/selection/` (codon models, RELAX, the codon alignment and its
validation) and `results/constraint/` (the per-residue tables, the orthologue
sets, the variant tables and the painted structures). The per-residue
deliverable is one table per human paralogue,
`constraint_<gene>_<accession>.tsv`, giving every residue in its own UniProt
numbering with four conservation layers, the occupancy each is conditional
on, its element, and whether it is a measured IP₃ contact, filter or gate
residue; `variants.tsv` joins the same columns onto every harvested ClinVar
record. These scores stratify variants of uncertain significance against the
labelled variants of the same gene. They are not pathogenicity calls and
should not be used as such. All primary data are public: genome assemblies
from NCBI Datasets, protein sequences from UniProt, the structure 6DQN and
the painted cryo-electron microscopy entries from the RCSB Protein Data Bank,
and variant records from ClinVar.

## Code availability

Every analysis is regenerated by the scripts in the repository
(`scripts/s9_*.py`, `scripts/s17_*.py`), each of which runs its constructed
negative controls before writing anything. This paper is rebuilt by
`python scripts/s26_assemble.py --paper constraint`, which re-verifies every
load-bearing number in it against the committed tables.
